terra.problem: A whole statue of gold suggests it was solid gold. The text calls it golden but does not specify its composition.
“No silver anywhere” goes beyond the text, which calls the statue golden without detailing its composition.
Calling the king “big on himself” adds an unmarked judgment about his character.
The explanation is a flat restatement of the measurement, without much of Papa Dorin's personality.
The full-band joke makes light of a command to worship the statue, a serious matter.
Saying singing sounds more fun makes light of the command to worship the statue.
The herald commanded the people; saying he asked for more softens the command.
The oven joke appears on a card about the threat of being thrown into a fiery furnace, a heavy moment.
The reference to the lions' den as another story in Daniel needs a Scripture reference.
“Everyone” goes beyond the text and overlooks the men who refused. The explanation also presents the crowd's feeling about the threat as fact.
The statement that Arioch is a name from the book of Daniel needs a Scripture reference.
The text identifies the king as the one who appointed these men; it does not say the herald never handed out jobs.
“Right there” adds a timing detail. The king speaks of what they should do when they hear the music, without saying it plays immediately.
The explanation drops the condition in the men's statement: they say that if the God they serve exists, He is able to deliver them.
The quiet-afternoon joke is on a card about deliverance from a deadly furnace and the king's hand.
The explanation omits the condition in the men's statement, presenting their words without the “if” in Daniel 3:17.
The burnt-cookie joke is attached to the king's order to heat the furnace for an act of violence.
Daniel 3:19 says the king ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter; it does not say that specific heat was reached.
“They never got the chance to run” adds a detail the text does not give.
The text does not say the king expected to see three men lying still.
The quotation uses “I” without first identifying the king as the speaker.
The claim that the book of Daniel has plenty of prophets is unsupported and has no reference.
The joke about a priest in the furnace makes light of deadly violence and speculates about what would have happened to him.
